description:
We’re NovaCore, a team bringing together game design, web development, and space science for NASA Space Apps Cairo 2026.

Our project, AstroBase Commander, is a proposed browser-based strategy game where players manage a Moon or Mars outpost. They’ll balance oxygen, power, food, and radiation protection and see how a decision in one system affects the rest. We plan to build a prototype with React and TypeScript and use NASA resources to inform the scenarios.

If you enjoy building.
summary: Mars Survival Academy is an educational game for kids aged 7–12 that turns real mission trade-offs into play. Players run a Mars outpost for 30 Sols with a limited daily power budget, so every building (life support, farming, radiation shielding, research) competes for the same energy and no choice is free. Space-weather alerts are grounded in real NASA data: a NASA DONKI solar energetic particle event and Curiosity MSL-RAD radiation measurements from NASA OSDR RadLab, shown in the game on a Data Sources screen. It answers the "Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer" challenge by letting young players feel why astronauts must balance power, oxygen and radiation protection, instead of only reading facts about them.
details:
What it does

Mars Survival Academy is a 2D top-down colony-management game for kids aged 7–12. The player is a trainee astronaut who must keep a Mars outpost alive for 30 Sols (Martian days). Three core meters are always visible: Energy, Oxygen and Shield (radiation protection). Food, water, ore and science are secondary resources.

How it works

Each Sol the outpost has a limited power budget. The player chooses from 7 structures, such as a solar panel, oxygen generator, water extractor, greenhouse, shield generator and research lab. Every structure has a construction cost and a power use, so helping one system (for example, powering the research lab) takes power from another (for example, shielding or oxygen). No choice is free. Space-weather alerts appear with a severity class and test the plan the player has built. At the end, a Mission Complete screen summarizes energy efficiency, atmospheric stability, radiation defense and colony status.

NASA data used

- NASA DONKI (Space Weather Database): a real solar energetic particle (SEP) event dated 2017-09-06 drives the in-game space-weather alert.

- NASA OSDR RadLab, MSL-RAD instrument on the Curiosity rover: daily mean absorbed dose rates measured on the Martian surface (7.68 µGy/h on 2017-09-06 and 17.87 µGy/h on 2017-09-11).

- Five short educational facts with source citations.

All of this data is archived, not live. It is labeled as archived NASA data in the game, and an in-game Data Sources screen lists every source. Power costs, production rates and shield effects are our own game design, built to teach the trade-off. They are not NASA figures.

Benefits

Kids experience the decisions behind a mission, not just its facts. The game uses plain language and short, repeatable play sessions, and can be used at home or in a classroom.

What we hope to achieve

We want young players to leave understanding one real constraint of deep-space survival: power, oxygen and radiation protection compete, and every choice has a cost.

Tools

Godot Engine and GDScript for the game, GitHub for version control and teamwork, and pixel-art UI and assets. We used AI tools (Claude and Manus) to help write and debug code and to draft text. The team reviewed and tested the results.
